brief.head: Brains, not stomachs
brief.text: Amit Varma re­jects over­pop­u­la­tion out­right. People move from sparse places to dense, pros­per­ous cities, vot­ing with their feet, and they are minds that cre­ate value, not mouths. {050-C01}

brief.head: A ₹300 helper
brief.text: Asked for some­thing under ₹10,000, Ajay Shah chose a ₹300 pill case. He fills it once a week, then obeys it like a zom­bie, no longer miss­ing doses. {#pillcase}

brief.head: Money follows child
brief.text: Large parts of India have left state schools for pri­vate ones, Ajay Shah said. Public money should fol­low the child, through vouch­ers, not re­ward only state-school pupils. {050-C05}

brief.head: One person, one vote
brief.text: Restrict vot­ing to those who pass a test? Amit Varma said no: “the mo­ment you cre­ate a bar, some­body de­cides what that bar is.” {050-C30}

brief.head: Kinky development
brief.text: Borrowing Lant Pritchett’s dis­tinc­tion, Amit Varma con­trasted na­tional de­vel­op­ment, end­ing poverty, with “kinky de­vel­op­ment”: small, neat ques­tions that ad­vance ca­reers. RCTs, he said, are the clas­sic ex­am­ple. {050-C16}

lead.kicker: At episode 50, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah take questions
lead.head: Fifty up, and no holds barred

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 50

body: For its fifti­eth episode, *Everything is Everything* turned the floor over to its lis­ten­ers. They sent ques­tions on Twitter and else­where, Ajay Shah sorted and short­ened them, and Amit Varma, for once, needed no notes.
The hosts had also moved. They had come to Bir, in Himachal Pradesh, for a week, to record ten episodes they are call­ing the Bir ses­sions. {#bir}
Shah ar­rived at the end of a hike, his first big out­ing after a frac­ture in January.
With so many ques­tions, Shah warned, the an­swers would be “like he­li­copter tours”. They ranged from blood and water to Bob Dylan, from the cen­tral bank to cry­ing at films.
## The case for growth
Two con­vic­tions ran under the tour. The first was that growth is the an­swer to poverty, and that the Indian state has often stood in its way.
Asked why India lost the gar­ment trade to Bangladesh, Shah said only about 35 per cent of work­ing-age Indians are em­ployed, among the worst rates in the world. {#employment}

Idle work­ers should bring wages down. Instead, he said, high min­i­mum wages and dense labour laws make big work­forces “dan­ger­ous and dif­fi­cult” to hire, so firms stay small and the fac­to­ries go to Bangladesh.

Degrowth got short shrift. “For a coun­try at the poverty lev­els of India, de­growth is just morally wrong,” Shah said. {050-C04} Varma called it a clas­sic lux­ury be­lief, held by the rich from air-conditioned rooms.
## The trou­ble with the state

The sec­ond con­vic­tion was scep­ti­cism of the state as it ac­tu­ally works. Most Indian state bod­ies, Shah said, are not in­sti­tu­tions but per­son­alised or­gan­i­sa­tions, which change with who­ever runs them. {050-C07}

The hosts’ one real dis­agree­ment came here. Shah often jus­ti­fies state ac­tion by point­ing to mar­ket fail­ure; Varma thinks mar­ket fail­ure rare and gov­ern­ment fail­ure ev­ery­where. Their val­ues, Varma said, are fully aligned.

Shah owned up to a change of mind. He once be­lieved Moore’s Law, Unix and the in­ter­net would make the world bet­ter. Now he thinks they add mag­ni­tude to what­ever peo­ple al­ready are, for good or for ill. {050-C21}
Varma, more op­ti­mistic about tech­nol­ogy and AI, called it a net pos­i­tive.
## Living well

The other half of the ques­tions were about life, and here the an­swers grew smaller in scale. Shah’s ad­vice to the young was to drop two habits: com­pet­ing with oth­ers, and liv­ing life as a per­for­mance.
Varma re­called a café in Bir the day be­fore, where he asked ev­ery­one when they were hap­pi­est. In the moun­tains, said one. With her dog, said an­other. When he has a new idea, said Shah.
Every an­swer, Varma no­ticed, was easy to reach. People who de­fine hap­pi­ness by grand goals, he said, are chas­ing some­thing elu­sive.
Not ev­ery­thing was serene. Varma ad­mit­ted he wastes hours on bul­let chess, and wishes he had never thought him­self in­tel­li­gent as a young man.
Shah, of­fered a genie, would send a bag of books back to the lead­ers of 1947.
Then the hosts thanked their lis­ten­ers. This was not two peo­ple talk­ing in a vac­uum, Varma said: “we’re hav­ing a con­ver­sa­tion with each other, but also in a sense with you.”
Shah had tried to end it ear­lier: “Amit, I’m starv­ing.” Varma stopped him to say good­bye to the lis­ten­ers first, then asked: “Should we go for lunch?”

second.head: Cliffhanger, solved

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the day Ajay Shah broke his leg

body: Asked whether he is ever ir­ra­tional and emo­tional, Ajay Shah said he is. But he does not rat­tle eas­ily, and he has a rule for crises: “the big­ger the cri­sis, the more calm and col­lected you need to be”. {#crisis}

Amit Varma had a story to prove it. On a hike, for the first time in 30 years or so, Shah had an ac­ci­dent: he fell off the edge of what ap­peared to be a moun­tain and was left hang­ing. {#thirtyyears}

His friend Ayush grabbed his hand. Shah was so pan­icked that his body was cov­ered in sweat. For about thirty sec­onds Ayush held him, and not a word passed be­tween them. Then Shah looked up and said: “Let’s solve this.” {050-S08}

quote.text: And then Ajay looked up at Ayush and said, Let’s solve this. So that’s Ajay Shah for you.

third.head: Mask on, reflux off

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his CPAP machine

body: A lis­tener asked Amit Varma about sleep ap­noea. His ad­vice: if you snore, get tested. He thought some­thing like 20 per cent of peo­ple have the prob­lem. {#apnea}
It stops your breath­ing in sleep, so you wake with­out re­al­is­ing and are tired by day. Obesity, an issue for him, can cause it.

Varma tested pos­i­tive for a mild case and took to a CPAP ma­chine. It trans­formed his life in an un­ex­pected way. Sleep had never been his trou­ble. Acid re­flux had: for years he woke with a cold or a sore throat.

The air gush­ing in through a nasal mask, he found, keeps the acid down. The morn­ing sore throats stopped. {050-S02} Still, he would not tell ev­ery­one with re­flux to buy one: “I don’t re­ally know what to make of it.”

sections.label: Making a living
sections.head: Reach first, revenue later
sections.caption: reach and revenue
body: Rishav Datta asked Amit Varma what he does for a liv­ing. “I’m a pro­fes­sional pod­caster as of now,” Varma said. Ajay Shah of­fered a gloss: “you’re just giv­ing gifts to the uni­verse.”

Varma thinks of the cre­ator econ­omy in terms of two Rs, reach and rev­enue. {050-C09} The pod­cast gives him reach, reach builds cred­i­bil­ity, and rev­enue comes from some­where. Much of it was, and is, his writ­ing course, the Art of Clear Writing, which he said has had some 2,500 stu­dents. {#students}
Early stu­dents came be­cause of his pod­cast and blog; now they come by word of mouth. But what­ever you do, for reach or rev­enue, he said, you have to put your heart and soul into it.
## Own your read­ers

Asked how to build a ca­reer in long-form jour­nal­ism, Varma was frank. India lacks out­lets like *The New Yorker* or *The Atlantic*, and beat re­porters have van­ished. In his friend Prem Panicker’s words, jour­nal­ism ends up “a mile wide and an inch deep”. {050-J11}

His ad­vice to any writer is to start a news­let­ter. Wait for news­pa­pers and you write rarely, within word counts and news cy­cles, with your read­ers scat­tered. “That email data­base be­longs to you,” he said, “not to a Substack or to any other news­let­ter site.” {050-C10}
~ Doing what he loves with­out com­pro­mise, he said, took decades. The shows re­main a labour of love: he doubts he is net pos­i­tive from them in money. {#netpositive}

quote.text: You have to think of what you do in terms of two Rs. One is reach and one is rev­enue.

art.caption: Amit Varma on reach and revenue

sections.label: The economy
sections.head: Stitched up by the state
sections.caption: India’s lost garment trade
body: Why did India lose the gar­ment trade to Bangladesh? Ajay Shah began with a num­ber: only about 35 per cent of work­ing-age Indians are em­ployed, among the worst rates any­where. {#employment}

So many idle hands should drive wages down. Instead, high min­i­mum wages and labour laws deter big work­forces. In Bangladesh, he said, the min­i­mum wage is 8,000, “so peo­ple get jobs”, and firms from all over the world build fac­to­ries there. {#eastbengal}
Amit Varma spelt out the arith­metic. Set a min­i­mum wage of ₹15,000, and a worker who would have had a job at ₹12,000 does not get one at all. {#minwage} It hurts “the poor­est of the poor”.
## Grow first
Degrowth, Shah said, is morally wrong for a coun­try as poor as India, whose in­come per per­son, ad­justed for pur­chas­ing power, is about a tenth of America’s. {050-C04}

He sorted capitalism’s ills by cause. Low wages and poor con­di­tions yield to growth: the poor­est fac­tory is hot, a richer one gets fans, a richer one still is air-conditioned. Pollution is an ex­ter­nal­ity, to be met with taxes, Coasean bar­gains or the state.

~ Varma called de­growth a lux­ury be­lief, and pointed to Bjorn Lomborg’s *The Skeptical Environmentalist*: London, a cen­tury ago, was pol­luted and un­healthy, and cleaned up as it grew pros­per­ous. {050-R10}

quote.text: So India has a self-inflicted wound of an ar­ti­fi­cially low work­ing pop­u­la­tion and ar­ti­fi­cially small econ­omy

art.caption: Ajay Shah on India’s lost garment trade

sections.label: Learning
sections.head: Right book, right moment
sections.caption: the right book at the right time
body: Five lis­ten­ers asked, in one form or an­other, how the hosts know so much. Amit Varma started with dis­trac­tion. His phone greys out Twitter and Instagram after half an hour a day each.

Then read, take notes, and book­mark the best minds on Twitter, fil­ing the book­marks in fold­ers to re­visit. “You play Candy Crush for an hour, your fu­ture self is stu­pider,” he said; read for an hour and you make your fu­ture self smarter. {050-C12}

Ajay Shah added pur­pose. Chase a job or fame and you may get it, and then what? “Life is too long to run on such mid­dle level goals.” {050-C13} He also urged in­vest­ing in your “five, fif­teen, fifty peo­ple”, and learn­ing by ad­ja­cen­cies.
## The match­ing process

Shah doubts there is an ob­jec­tively great book. We change through time, so the trick is to en­gage lightly with many and keep a men­tal index, until the right one ar­rives at the right time. {050-C11}

Two of his came from Lant Pritchett: *Seeing Like a State* and *The Functions of the Executive*, a 1938 man­age­ment book. His moral: “gen­tle reader, hang out with peo­ple who know great books.” {050-S05}
~ Learning India, he said, is not like learn­ing physics. Look out of the win­dow, and no­tice how the gen­der mix of flights changes with the time of day. {050-C14}

quote.text: And what we need is the match­ing process where the right book shows up at the right time.

art.caption: Amit Varma on the right book at the right time

sections.label: The state
sections.head: People go, the rules stay
sections.caption: institutions and organisations
body: In India, Ajay Shah said, the word “in­sti­tu­tion” is bandied about too loosely. An in­sti­tu­tion is an im­per­sonal ca­pa­bil­ity: peo­ple come and go, but it be­haves in a pre­dictable and con­sis­tent way. {050-C07}

Hindustan Lever, where CEOs come and go, qual­i­fies. Most Indian state bod­ies do not: they are per­son­alised or­gan­i­sa­tions. For RBI to emerge as an in­sti­tu­tion, he said, India needed the legal changes for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing.

Why ac­cept a cen­tral bank fix­ing the short-term in­ter­est rate? Shah an­swered from first prin­ci­ples: money solves the dou­ble co­in­ci­dence of wants, and “the only recipe we know to make money in­volves the cen­tral bank pick­ing a num­ber for the in­ter­est rate at the short end”. {050-C06}
## Unlucky in 1947

Given a genie’s wish, Shah would re­visit 1947, an un­lucky year. India’s founders were formed be­tween 1927 and 1947, when free­dom did badly world­wide and war economies made total state mo­bil­i­sa­tion nor­mal. {050-C27}

He would take Nehru, Gandhi, Rajagopalachari and oth­ers a bag of books. The new state, he said, should have spent about 10 per cent of GDP on ba­sics: rule of law, the ju­di­ciary, a tax sys­tem with rule of law.
~ Amit Varma doubted that books alone would have changed minds formed over decades. Shah’s own con­ver­sion by *Seeing Like a State*, he said, came at the right time.

quote.text: I feel that we just got very, very un­lucky in the great free­dom move­ment gen­er­a­tion, where I think 1947 was an un­lucky year.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on institutions and organisations

sections.label: Freedom
sections.head: No Ram Rajya on offer
sections.caption: spontaneous order and its ills
body: A lis­tener pressed the point: pa­tri­archy, caste and global warm­ing are prod­ucts of spon­ta­neous order too. Ajay Shah’s first an­swer was to drop utopia. “There will be no Ram Rajya.” {050-J17}

Global warm­ing, he said, is a mar­ket fail­ure that calls for state ac­tion. Social evils must change from the bot­tom up, be­cause what is im­posed from the top may not work and is “truly dan­ger­ous be­cause who knows what the val­ues and the cul­ture of the peo­ple at the top are”. {050-C15}

Amit Varma called spon­ta­neous order a de­scrip­tion, not a ver­dict. The world still has sex­ism, he said, but it is much bet­ter for women than a cen­tury ago, through mar­kets and chang­ing val­ues rather than the lazy call for an­other law.
## Markets against caste

On caste, Varma drew on Tony Joseph and David Reich: some 2,000 years of en­forced caste en­dogamy made India a col­lec­tion of small, closed pop­u­la­tions, shrink­ing net­works and breed­ing dis­eases found nowhere else. {050-C28}

His rem­edy echoes the Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad, whose two he­roes are Babasaheb Ambedkar and Adam Smith: growth and cities. When firms com­pete for work­ers and cus­tomers, dis­crim­i­na­tion gets costly.
~ This is also where the hosts part ways, a lit­tle. Shah often in­vokes mar­ket fail­ure; Varma thinks it rare. “Government fail­ure is ubiq­ui­tous,” he said. {050-C19}

quote.text: If you’re look­ing for a large pop­u­la­tion, look at the Han Chinese. But India is re­ally a col­lec­tion of thou­sands of small pop­u­la­tions.
quote.who: David Reich, as quoted by Amit Varma

art.caption: Ajay Shah on spontaneous order and its ills

sections.label: How to live
sections.head: Drop the race, skip the show
sections.caption: competition and performance
body: How should a young per­son find mean­ing? Ajay Shah’s an­swer was to stop two things: com­pet­ing to outdo class­mates and neigh­bours, and liv­ing “life as a per­for­mance” for so­cial media or the résumé. {050-C24}
Drop both, he said, and what is left is the stuff you value. The same habits, he thinks, are why he does not rat­tle eas­ily.

Amit Varma urged thought be­fore mar­ry­ing or hav­ing chil­dren: is it what you want, or René Girard’s mimetic de­sire, want­ing what oth­ers want? Choose com­mu­ni­ties by val­ues, not cir­cum­stance. His own lament: “I am cos­mopoli­tan but I’m not rooted enough.” {050-C23}
## The best at time T
Varma’s new rule is to end each year fit­ter and with more done. Shah de­murred: age­ing hap­pens “with prob­a­bil­ity one”. Better to aim to be “the best Amit Varma I can be at time T”. {050-C26}

For young peo­ple paral­ysed by op­tions, Varma of­fered Steve Jobs’s ad­vice to Jony Ive: learn to say no to things you love, then com­mit to one. {050-C25} Shah added: ap­pren­tice your­self to a pas­sion­ate mas­ter.
~ Varma closed with Richard Bach: “What a cater­pil­lar calls the end of the world, the mas­ter calls a but­ter­fly.” {050-J15}

quote.text: How you spend your days, of course, is how you spend your life.
quote.who: Annie Dillard, as quoted by Amit Varma

art.caption: Amit Varma on competition and performance

quote.text: And if there was good val­ues and good char­ac­ter in­side you, then the CPUs and the in­ter­net have taken that vec­tor and added mag­ni­tude to that vec­tor.

p3.title: Tales from Bir
p3.deck: Shirts, chess, a Haryanvi childhood and the weight of water

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on khadi, Udaipur and a wardrobe of gifts
stories.head: From khadi white to silk prints
body: A whole group of lis­ten­ers had ques­tions about Ajay Shah’s shirts. Mayank asked whether he buys them or is given them. Arpita asked how he chooses them, for nor­mal life and for the show. Eric Paul just wanted to know where to get them. {#shirts}

For years, Shah said, he wore a uni­form “stolen from the look” of the econ­o­mists Kirit Parikh and Shekhar Shah: a plain white or off-white shirt from Khadi Emporium, every sin­gle day of the year. {#uniform}

The sleeves were half, be­cause India is too hot for full sleeves, and it took him years to gain the con­fi­dence to give up full-sleeved shirts. He has worn a suit and tie abroad, he said, but never in his whole life in India.
Then, many years later, he stum­bled on printed shirts. He thinks it was at Udaipur. He bought a few, and it was “an in­ter­est­ing dif­fer­ent look”.

Around then the hosts got going on *Everything is Everything*, and Shah thought: why not ex­per­i­ment? He wore some of the printed shirts on the show, and they looked good. He bought more, and peo­ple began giv­ing them to him. “Most of my shirts are ac­tu­ally gifts.” {050-S10}
A cou­ple come from an Arvind re­tail out­let in Ahmedabad, and some came by mail order. Several are silk shirts from Indian Colours, printed with con­tem­po­rary Indian art.
~ He said he could give peo­ple a list of the sources.
stories.why: A bor­rowed uni­form gave way, late and al­most by ac­ci­dent, to a sig­na­ture look. Conventions can be dropped at any age: the show be­came the place to ex­per­i­ment, and most of what fol­lowed ar­rived as gifts. {050-S10}

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the battle with his own attention
stories.head: Sheepish in a coffee shop
body: Amit Varma banks episodes. He will go to Delhi and record eight episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen* in nine days, do the same in Bangalore, then have weeks free. {#bank}
Balance, he said, is not his prob­lem. Waste is. In the hours he sets aside for work, he gets dis­tracted and plays on­line bul­let chess for hours.

He has built a home of­fice he loves, sit-stand desk and all. He still goes to Starbucks to work, be­cause sit­ting there with a lap­top, “you feel a lit­tle sheep­ish about play­ing chess for an hour.” {050-S03}
~ “I strug­gle as much as you do,” he told lis­ten­ers. “It’s an on­go­ing bat­tle with dis­ci­pline and our own minds.”
stories.why: Discipline is often a mat­ter of where you sit rather than how hard you try. And the peo­ple who seem most pro­duc­tive, Varma ad­mit­ted, are fight­ing the same bat­tle as ev­ery­one else.
stories.postscript: His Chess.com bul­let rat­ing, he said, rises about 100 points on keto or modafinil days, and falls back when he stops. {050-S04}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on working from Starbucks

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Vinay Singhal and the future of dialects
stories.head: A thousand true fans for Haryanvi
body: Vinay Singhal grew up in a Haryana vil­lage, Amit Varma re­called from his episode with him, and twice in his life he had to try re­ally hard.
The first time was when he joined an English-medium school in the eighth stan­dard. He didn’t know English prop­erly, worked at it and reached the top of his class. {#vinay}
The sec­ond came when he moved to a city, prob­a­bly Delhi, Varma thought. Now the prob­lem was Hindi: at home he had spo­ken Haryanvi. That is the great flat­ten­ing, as di­alects give way in towns.
~ Yet Singhal’s ven­ture, STAGE, makes con­tent in Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and Maithili. Online, the long tail sur­vives, be­cause “every di­alect will at least have a thou­sand true fans”. {050-S07}
stories.why: Two forces pull on India’s lan­guages: a flat­ten­ing to­wards Hindi and English, and an in­ter­net that re­wards niches. Varma’s ad­vice to new pod­cast­ers fol­lows: if your other lan­guage is nearly as good as your English, use it.
stories.postscript: His hope: that the great flat­ten­ing be­comes “a mere echo from the past”.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Vinay Singhal’s two languages

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on six litres of blood and a training trick
stories.head: Thin on water, thick in blood
body: An av­er­age human body holds six litres of blood, Ajay Shah said. Sweat out a litre and you lose 16.66 per cent of it, which is ma­te­rial. The blood thick­ens, and the heart works harder. {050-S01}

That is why de­hy­drated ex­er­cise feels so tir­ing, and why water brings re­lief. Shah’s twist: on a tread­mill, with a fridge of water nearby, you could de­lib­er­ately train short of water to push your heart harder.
Amit Varma saw an open­ing. “The Bengali in me is freak­ing de­lighted,” he said: he could stay away from water, walk around gen­tly, and still work his heart. {050-J01}
~ Then he turned se­ri­ous. Having once read some twenty to forty run­ning books in a cou­ple of months, he warned that in marathons a lot of peo­ple die from drink­ing too much.

quote.text: So the blood be­comes thicker. When the blood is thicker, it is harder for the heart to pump that blood.

quiz.q: What distinguishes an institution from a mere organisation, in Ajay Shah’s definition?
quiz.a: It works pre­dictably and con­sis­tently, who­ever comes and goes: an im­per­sonal ca­pa­bil­ity.

quiz.q: Which phrase did Amit Varma borrow from Lant Pritchett to describe small questions that advance careers?
quiz.a: Kinky de­vel­op­ment, as op­posed to na­tional de­vel­op­ment, with RCTs the clas­sic ex­am­ple.

quiz.q: Whose look did Ajay Shah’s old uniform of plain white khadi shirts copy?
quiz.a: The econ­o­mists Kirit Parikh and Shekhar Shah: Khadi Emporium shirts, half-sleeved.

quiz.q: Which law explains, for Ajay Shah, why Indian parents push their children towards English?
quiz.a: Metcalfe’s law: a network’s value grows with the square of its nodes.

glossary.def: Wanting some­thing be­cause other peo­ple want it, in René Girard’s phrase.
Children an av­er­age woman would have at a sin­gle year’s rates.
A network’s value grows with the square of its nodes.
Marrying only within one’s own caste or sub­caste.
Barter’s prob­lem: each side must want what the other has.
Lant Pritchett’s term for small ques­tions with easy, ca­reer-friendly an­swers.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 50. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); George Orwell (Cassowary Colorizations, CC BY 2.0); Ingmar Bergman (Joost Evers / Anefo, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple, Open Library, Spotify and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Wild Strawberries
shelf.creator: Ingmar Bergman
shelf.why: Amit thinks it is the best way into Bergman, who can feel in­ac­ces­si­ble.

shelf.title: Primers on public choice, classical liberalism, Hayek and Friedman
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: A short, mas­ter­ful in­tro­duc­tion to pub­lic choice the­ory, read­able in under an hour, that ex­plains why state fail­ure is prac­ti­cally ev­ery­where though ev­ery­one talks only of mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C. Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: Against the Grain
shelf.creator: James C. Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how agri­cul­ture and grain-based early states made life worse for or­di­nary peo­ple, over­turn­ing the story of steady progress.

shelf.title: The Functions of the Executive
shelf.creator: Chester Barnard
shelf.why: Chester Barnard’s book opened Ajay’s think­ing on or­gan­i­sa­tional be­hav­iour and on what goes wrong in large, com­plex or­gan­i­sa­tions, firms and gov­ern­ments alike.

shelf.title: Essays
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: Orwell’s non­fic­tion, which Amit prefers to the nov­els: a chrono­log­i­cal look at Orwell the thinker, who banged out three or four bril­liant col­umns a week.

shelf.title: Order without Design
shelf.creator: Alain Bertaud
shelf.why: Amit’s desert-island book on cities: Bertaud brings eco­nom­ics and many other dis­ci­plines to urban plan­ning, ex­poses the fol­lies of high mod­ernism and re­spects the local knowl­edge be­hind why streets and cities work as they do.

shelf.title: Population Is Not a Problem, but Our Greatest Strength
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s chal­lenge to the school les­son that pop­u­la­tion is India’s big­gest prob­lem: peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs, pop­u­la­tion den­sity drives pros­per­ity, and the ills blamed on pop­u­la­tion are fail­ures of gov­er­nance.

shelf.title: Milton Friedman on the minimum wage
shelf.creator: Milton Friedman
shelf.why: Friedman’s short video ar­gu­ment that a min­i­mum wage doesn’t lift a low-productivity worker’s pay to the legal floor: it makes the job il­le­gal, so the wage drops to zero.

shelf.title: The Skeptical Environmentalist
shelf.creator: Bjorn Lomborg
shelf.why: Lomborg traces how great Western cities like London, once as filthy and un­healthy as any Indian city today, cleaned up as they got richer.

shelf.title: Saumya Roy’s book on the trash mountains of Bombay
shelf.creator: Saumya Roy
shelf.why: Ajay calls it amaz­ing.

shelf.title: Hardcore History
shelf.creator: Dan Carlin
shelf.why: One man reads around forty books per episode and then sim­ply talks, with no script, co-host or sound ef­fects, and it is riv­et­ing.

shelf.title: Making Sense
shelf.creator: Sam Harris
shelf.why: Sam Harris’s con­ver­sa­tion pod­cast, which Amit rec­om­mends for the art of con­ver­sa­tion: he learned a lot about pod­cast­ing from its flow and rhythm in the early days, though it is now mostly pay­walled and Harris has moved in dif­fer­ent di­rec­tions.

shelf.title: Ideas of India
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: He thinks she does an in­cred­i­ble job.

shelf.title: Grand Tamasha
shelf.creator: Milan Vaishnav
shelf.why: Vaishnav is a fine thinker, and the pod­cast is a good way to fol­low Indian pol­i­tics.

shelf.title: When Crime Pays
shelf.creator: Milan Vaishnav
shelf.why: A must-read on crime in Indian pol­i­tics.

shelf.title: EconTalk
shelf.creator: Russ Roberts
shelf.why: Russ Roberts’s pod­cast, a long-time favourite of Amit’s and the clos­est to his own ap­proach: re­laxed, con­ver­sa­tional and deep, fo­cused on ideas rather than the guest’s life.

shelf.title: Early Indians
shelf.creator: Tony Joseph
shelf.why: Tony Joseph uses the genes of liv­ing peo­ple to re­con­struct thou­sands of years of Indian his­tory: the first Indians, the Harappans, the Aryan mi­gra­tion, and how caste en­dogamy set in about 2,000 years ago after mil­len­nia of in­ter­min­gling.

shelf.title: Who We Are and How We Got Here
shelf.creator: David Reich
shelf.why: Reich ex­plains how full-genome stud­ies re­con­struct human his­tory and over­turned re­ceived wis­dom from ar­chae­ol­ogy.

shelf.title: Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study
shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: It asks whether such poli­cies ac­tu­ally helped the peo­ple they were meant to help.

shelf.title: Wanderers, Kings, Merchants
shelf.creator: Peggy Mohan
shelf.why: Peggy Mohan reads India’s past through its liv­ing lan­guages, doing with lan­guage what Reich and Joseph did with genes: mi­grat­ing men mar­ried local women, so chil­dren spoke their mothers’ tongue first, and Sanskrit ab­sorbed local sounds such as retroflexes.

shelf.title: Profit = Philanthropy
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that in a world of vol­un­tary ex­change the only way to profit is by mak­ing some­one else bet­ter off, which makes profit an in­cen­tive to do good and the high­est form of phi­lan­thropy.

shelf.title: Determinants of Trade Misinvoicing
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta, Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s co-authored paper mea­sur­ing how Indian busi­nesses mis­in­voiced trade on a stag­ger­ing scale to get around ex­change con­trols and achieve de facto con­vert­ibil­ity, which shows that cap­i­tal con­trols fail.

shelf.title: Praise for intelligence can undermine children’s motivation and performance
shelf.creator: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck
shelf.why: The study be­hind Amit’s ad­vice to ‘focus on verbs, not adjectives’: chil­dren praised for being smart later tried less and even cheated, while chil­dren praised for ef­fort kept im­prov­ing.

shelf.title: Wanting
shelf.creator: Luke Burgis
shelf.why: Burgis brings René Girard’s mimetic de­sire into ev­ery­day life: we want things be­cause oth­ers want them.

shelf.title: A Meditation on Form
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s essay on how form dic­tates con­tent: long-form pod­cast­ing is a dif­fer­ent ac­tiv­ity from short-form, not a longer ver­sion of it, and its pa­tience, lis­ten­ing and cu­rios­ity changed him as a host and per­haps as a per­son.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen: eight-hour episode with Jerry Pinto
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An eight-and-a-half-hour oral his­tory that Amit calls per­haps his most mem­o­rable, and the episode through which many lis­ten­ers find the show.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen: eight-hour episode with KP Krishnan
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything: the hiking episode
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay on his pas­sion for hik­ing, from the Goecha La trek be­neath Kanchenjunga to why the worst ac­ci­dents hap­pen when you think you’re al­most home.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything: the declutter episode (episode 30)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Much of the hosts’ per­sonal phi­los­o­phy of life: recog­nise your con­straints, es­pe­cially time, pri­ori­tise ac­cord­ingly, and pre­fer pro­cesses to grand goals.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: A weekly pill case
shelf.why: He fills it once a week and then fol­lows it with­out think­ing.

shelf.title: Indian Colours
shelf.why: The source of many of Ajay’s art shirts: it prints con­tem­po­rary Indian art on shirts, cups and stoles and pays artists roy­al­ties, so or­di­nary peo­ple can sur­round them­selves with beauty with­out spend­ing lakhs on orig­i­nals.

shelf.title: Blue
shelf.creator: Joni Mitchell
shelf.why: Amit’s favourite Joni Mitchell album, by a singer-songwriter and gui­tarist ahead of her time whose polio-shaped gui­tar play­ing fits no sin­gle genre.

shelf.title: New York
shelf.creator: Lou Reed
shelf.why: Where to start with Lou Reed.

shelf.title: Blood on the Tracks
shelf.creator: Bob Dylan
shelf.why: One of his two spe­cific favourites, from dif­fer­ent phases of Dylan’s life.

shelf.title: Time Out of Mind
shelf.creator: Bob Dylan
shelf.why: Amit’s favourite Dylan album, a prime ex­am­ple of late-career mas­tery.

shelf.title: Astral Weeks
shelf.creator: Van Morrison
shelf.why: Van Morrison’s mas­ter­piece of deeply mov­ing songs, born when the pro­ducer re­placed his mu­si­cians with jazz play­ers, in­clud­ing bassist Richard Davis, who im­pro­vised around him.

shelf.title: Moondance
shelf.creator: Van Morrison
shelf.why: The coun­ter­point to Astral Weeks: Van Morrison with his own band, doing R&B the tra­di­tional way, ex­actly as he wanted.

laughs.text: After Ajay ex­plains how de­hy­dra­tion makes the heart work harder, Amit says: ‘The Bengali in me is freak­ing de­lighted be­cause I’m just think­ing that I don’t need to go run­ning any­more. I can just stay away from water and walk around gen­tly and the heart is still work­ing for you.’ Ajay replies: ‘More chal­leng­ing than walk­ing around gen­tly when well hy­drated.’

Ajay’s the­ory of cin­ema: ‘the qual­ity of movies in a coun­try is ba­si­cally pro­por­tional to the me­dian age. So when India was a very young coun­try, the qual­ity of the movies was atro­cious.’ He later con­cludes that young peo­ple ‘give us bad movies’ but are great for so­ci­ety. Amit re­sponds by rec­om­mend­ing Wild Strawberries.

Ajay asks whether, once he has made Amit a mas­ter pro­gram­mer, Amit would cry at a beau­ti­ful al­go­rithm. Amit: ‘Tears are com­ing to my eyes think­ing of the amount of brute co­er­cion that would be re­quired to make me a mas­ter of com­puter pro­gram­ming.’
Reading out a lis­tener ques­tion from Vaishnav Vyas, who shoots the show: ‘Vaishnav Vyas. I won­der who that is.’ Amit: ‘I won­der who that is.’
Nehru’s re­mark to J.R.D. Tata, ‘Do not speak to me of profit. It is a dirty word’, which Amit says Nehru got com­pletely wrong.
